note: Supporting evidence only. The internal thresholds in docs/03-GOOGLE-RESILIENCE.md are OUR standards and are not derived from, or claimed to be, Google thresholds. None of the sources below contradicts docs/03. Google documentation changes often, so re-verify before any material policy decision.

records.claim: Google's spam policies define doorway abuse as sites or pages created to rank for specific, similar queries that lead users to intermediate pages, and give region- or city-targeted pages and domains that funnel users onward as an example.
records.source_title: Spam policies for Google web search
records.evidence_summary: The doorway abuse section describes pages made to rank for similar queries that act as funnels. Its examples include multiple domains or pages targeting specific regions or cities.
records.limitations: Page 'last updated' date is shown. The policy is qualitative and publishes no numeric thresholds.

records.claim: Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages primarily to manipulate rankings, including using generative AI to create many pages without adding value.
records.source_title: Spam policies for Google web search
records.evidence_summary: The scaled content abuse section targets many pages made mainly to manipulate rankings, however they are produced, and explicitly includes generative-AI page generation without added value.

records.claim: Google's people-first content guidance asks whether content gives original information, research, or analysis and substantial value beyond other sources, shows clear sourcing and expertise, is made for people rather than search engines, and avoids extensive automation. It suggests explaining 'Who, How, and Why', including how AI or automation was used.
records.evidence_summary: The self-assessment questions cover originality, added value, expertise and trust (E-E-A-T), and people-first versus search-first intent. The Who/How/Why section suggests being transparent about authorship and about how automation or AI was used.
records.limitations: The guidance is self-assessment, not a checklist Google publishes as a ranking formula. The AI-use disclosure suggestion is not yet reflected in docs/04; recorded as an open question, not a contradiction.

records.claim: Google's documented position is that appropriate use of AI or automation is not in itself against its guidelines. Quality, helpfulness, and purpose matter, and using AI mainly to manipulate rankings violates spam policy.
records.source_title: Google Search's guidance about AI-generated content
records.evidence_summary: Google rewards helpful content however it was produced, does not ban AI-assisted content, and treats AI used mainly to manipulate rankings as spam.
records.limitations: Blog post dated February 2023 (day not re-confirmed). Its position is consistent with the 2025 documentation in goog-005.

records.claim: Google's guidance on generative AI content allows its use but warns that generating many pages without added value may violate the scaled content abuse policy. It recommends accuracy (including for auto-generated metadata and structured data) and suggests considering disclosure of how content was created.
records.source_title: Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website
records.evidence_summary: Gen AI is permitted but tied to the scaled content abuse policy. The page stresses accuracy and relevance for generated titles, descriptions, structured data, and alt text, and notes that sharing how content was created can give readers context.
records.limitations: Some sections (e.g., AI image metadata) apply to e-commerce and are not directly relevant.

records.claim: Google's guide to generative AI features in Search recommends unique, non-commodity content that generic AI cannot easily reproduce. It warns against creating pages for every query variation (scaled content abuse), says GEO/AEO 'hacks' such as llms.txt files, artificial chunking, or rewriting for AI do not help, and says core SEO best practices still apply.
records.source_title: Google's guide to optimizing for generative AI features on Google Search
records.evidence_summary: The guide contrasts commodity summaries with first-hand, expert, non-commodity content. It warns that creating pages for fan-out query variations can violate scaled content abuse, lists GEO/AEO misconceptions, and states that its generative features are rooted in core Search ranking and quality systems. Announced on the Search Central Blog on 2026-05-15.
records.limitations: The guide recommends Google Business Profile for local businesses. That applies only to genuine local businesses; our non-negotiables forbid a fake GBP. This is consistent with, not in tension with, docs.

records.claim: Google announced its generative-AI optimization resource on the Search Central Blog in May 2026.
records.source_title: A new resource for optimizing for generative AI in Google Search
records.evidence_summary: The announcement post for the guide in goog-006.
records.limitations: Date taken from search-result metadata. The post body was not separately opened.
